title: Hip-Hop
subtitle: Bounce first. Every step in this style is the bounce plus one idea.
description: Hip-hop is the widest style in the catalog, and the reason beginners stall in it is that there is no obvious order — the party steps, the funk styles and the choreo classes all look like starting points. They are not. Get the bounce into your body, learn to isolate one part at a time, then work through the old-school vocabulary the whole style is quoting. The funk branches (popping, locking, waving) and the travelling walks come off that trunk, and the choreo stage is where the vocabulary turns into sentences.

stages.title: Get the bounce
stages.description: The pulse everything else sits on. Hip-hop is a down-groove — you hit the beat by dropping into it, not by lifting off it. If you skip this stage every later step will look like an exercise instead of a dance.

steps.title: The bounce
steps.description: Knees soft, weight down, chest answering the beat. Learn it standing on the spot and keep it running underneath every other step on this path.

steps.title: Head nod
steps.description: The bounce read from the neck up. It looks like nothing and it is the difference between dancing to the track and counting along with it.

steps.title: Two step
steps.description: Side to side, weight fully transferring, bounce intact. The default hip-hop step and the thing you return to between everything else.

steps.title: Rock steady grooves
steps.description: The Pork Chop, the Leo Walk and the Bump — the grooves the Rock Steady Crew put into the vocabulary. Four ways to rock the same pulse before you own any footwork.

stages.title: Isolate it
stages.description: Move one part of your body while the rest stays quiet. This is the stage people skip and the reason their steps look stiff — the party dances in stage three are all isolations with a name attached.

steps.title: Chest pop
steps.description: Punch the chest forward and release, shoulders out of it. Your first accent, and the base of half the moves in this style.

steps.title: Body roll
steps.description: Ripple the isolation down through head, chest and hips as one continuous line. Practise it in eight slow counts before you try it at tempo.

steps.title: Hip roll
steps.description: The same rolling motion driven from the hips, feet flat. Where the body roll gets its bottom half.

steps.title: Hip swivel
steps.description: Also called the Indian Step: kick, switch and twist the hips against the direction of travel. The first step where the top and bottom half disagree on purpose.

steps.title: Arm wave
steps.description: Isolate every joint from shoulder to fingertip and fire them in sequence. Drill the joints separately first — a wave is a control exercise before it is a move.

stages.title: Old-school foundation
stages.description: The party dances from the eighties and nineties. Learn them because everything newer is quoting them, and because a freestyle without vocabulary is just a bounce with nowhere to go. Start with the guided tour, then take the steps one at a time.

steps.title: Tour the old-school steps
steps.description: Fifteen classic steps demonstrated back to back with their names. Watch it once for the map, then come back to it whenever a step name means nothing to you.

steps.title: The prep
steps.description: The Kid 'n Play bounce-and-reach. The cleanest place to start because it is almost pure groove with an arm on top.

steps.title: Running man
steps.description: Slide one foot back as the other knee drives up. The single most recognisable step in the style — get the weight transfer clean before you speed it up.

steps.title: Roger rabbit
steps.description: The running man travelling backwards with a hop. Same mechanics, reversed — which is exactly why it goes after it and not before.

steps.title: The reebok
steps.description: A bouncing shuffle with the arms pumping across the body. Fast, low and the easiest of these to hide a mistake in.

steps.title: Cabbage patch
steps.description: Circle both arms in front of you over a rocking bounce. Pure upper body — a good one to drill while your legs recover.

steps.title: The wop
steps.description: Alternating arm sweeps with a chest bounce behind them. Sits right next to the cabbage patch and swaps in for it mid-freestyle.

steps.title: The smurf
steps.description: A side-to-side bounce with the arms crossing over. One of the oldest party steps here and still one of the most useful for filling eight counts.

steps.title: Bart simpson
steps.description: Hop and swing the arms across in front. Comes with a full breakdown, a practice pass and a variation — the most thoroughly taught step on this path.

steps.title: Biz markie
steps.description: A stomping step with a shoulder shrug behind it. Same lesson structure as the bart simpson, so learn them in the same session.

steps.title: The chicken / monastery
steps.description: Hands in, knees bouncing out, elbows doing the work. Learn the chicken and the monastery variation together — the tutorial compares them directly.

stages.title: Pop, lock and wave
stages.description: The funk styles hip-hop borrows from. They are separate traditions with their own rules, but every hip-hop freestyle raids them, and the control they teach transfers straight back into your grooves.

steps.title: The hit
steps.description: Popping's whole foundation: tense a muscle hard enough to snap, then release, on the beat. Find the forearm tendon first — if you can pop that, you can pop anywhere.

steps.title: Waving through the body
steps.description: Take the arm wave across the chest and out the other side. Three angles, one continuous line, no visible seams at the shoulders.

steps.title: Boogaloo
steps.description: The rolling, boneless counterpart to the hit — hips and knees circling while the hits punctuate. Popping's two halves, and most people only ever learn one.

steps.title: The robot
steps.description: Dime stops: travel a limb, then kill it dead. A full routine built from pivots and stops — the clearest test of whether your hit is actually clean.

steps.title: The muscleman lock
steps.description: Locking's signature freeze: arms up, everything stops at once. The lock is the point — the travel between locks barely matters.

steps.title: Uncle sam point
steps.description: Throw the point out and lock behind it. Your first locking move that goes somewhere instead of holding still.

steps.title: Punch and clap
steps.description: Punches and claps threaded between the locks. This is where locking starts sounding like music instead of looking like poses.

stages.title: Walks and glides
stages.description: Everything so far happens on one spot. These cover ground, and most of them are illusions — the audience should not be able to tell which foot is carrying you.

steps.title: The moonwalk
steps.description: Drag one foot back while the other rolls heel to toe. The most attempted move in dance and the one most often given up on after ten minutes — slow it right down.

steps.title: Side glide
steps.description: The same trick sideways, feet swapping which one hides the push. Builds through footwork, then the illusion, then full speed.

steps.title: Air walk
steps.description: Walk forward while travelling nowhere. Needs the glide's weight control or it collapses into ordinary steps.

steps.title: Wiggle walk
steps.description: Mr Wiggles' travelling step: the swivel taken forward, hips leading, upper body loose.

steps.title: C-walk
steps.description: The west-coast walk — quick pivots on the balls of the feet that trace a letter on the floor. All ankle, no knee.

steps.title: Heel-toe walk out
steps.description: Split the feet out on the heels and back in on the toes. Basic footwork that shows up inside half the choreo you will be given.

stages.title: New-school social steps
stages.description: The ones people actually do at a party. They are easier than stage three and they age faster, but knowing them is the difference between watching a floor and joining it.

steps.title: The dougie
steps.description: Lean, rock and run a hand through your hair. Barely a step — almost entirely attitude, which is the skill it teaches.

steps.title: Milly rock
steps.description: Alternating arm rocks over a shoulder bounce. Built up arms first, then body, then feet — a good model for how to learn any of these.

steps.title: Stanky leg
steps.description: Plant one leg and wobble the other from the knee down. Your first move built entirely on one loose joint.

steps.title: Nae nae
steps.description: Bend, step back, arm up high. Three counts and done — learn it for the transition into the whip.

steps.title: The whip
steps.description: Throw the arm out over a leaning bounce. Pairs with the nae nae by design; the same tutorial adds the superman on top.

steps.title: Harlem shake
steps.description: Shoulders shuddering fast and loose over a held stance. Needs the isolation work from stage two — without it the whole torso shakes and the move disappears.

stages.title: Put it together
stages.description: Steps are vocabulary. These are sentences. Work up the length — a five-minute combo, a beginner routine, then a full class — and finish by throwing the counts away.

steps.title: Lunge and running man combo
steps.description: Five minutes, two moves, one phrase. The smallest possible thing that is more than a step.

steps.title: First full routine
steps.description: A short beginner routine with jumps, rocks, corners and a kick ball change — taught slowly, then with music. The first time the bounce has to survive a whole track.

steps.title: A full class
steps.description: Twenty minutes of class: warm-up, phrase, repeat, run. Longer than anything above it and the first one that will actually make you sweat.

steps.title: Choreo to a track
steps.description: A beginner routine set to one song end to end. Learning choreography is its own skill — picking phrases up fast is separate from knowing moves.

steps.title: Long-form choreography
steps.description: Three parts, each broken down, recapped and run to slow music before it speeds up. Thirty-plus minutes of tutorial — treat it as a week of practice, not a session.

steps.title: Crew-style choreography
steps.description: A Jabbawockeez routine with a tutorial attached. Precision work — the funk-style control from stage four is what makes the hits land together.

steps.title: Freestyle a track end to end
steps.description: No counts, no mirror, no routine. One track, bounce running the whole way through, and you change step whenever the music tells you to. Everything above this exists to give you something to reach for when it does — this is the actual goal of the path.
